GraphSession:
Context manager that records CAD operations into a DAG.

Usage::

    with GraphSession() as session:
        n1 = record_operation(
            "make_line_redge", {"start": (0, 0, 0), "end": (1, 0, 0)}
        )
        n2 = record_operation(
            "make_line_redge", {"start": (1, 0, 0), "end": (1, 1, 0)}
        )
        record_operation(
            "make_wire_from_edges_rwire", {"edge_count": 2}, inputs=[n1, n2]
        )

    # Access the graph after the session
    print(session.graph.topological_order())

Args:
    graph_id: Id of the recorded graph (random when omitted).
    allow_external_definitions: Let built ``Part``/``Assembly`` values
        that carry their own definition enter as ``reference_definition``
        nodes instead of being rejected.
    namespace: Prefix for every node and object id this session
        allocates, as in ``OperationGraph(namespace=...)``.
    shared_lineage: Accept values recorded by other sessions with the
        same ``graph_id`` by adopting their nodes, as in
        ``OperationGraph.adopt``. Notebook cell sessions use this;
        every other session only accepts nodes its own graph owns.

OperationGraph:
A directed acyclic graph of CAD operations.

The graph tracks nodes (operations) and edges (data-flow dependencies).
It supports topological ordering, upstream/downstream queries, and
root/leaf enumeration.

Usage::

    g = OperationGraph()
    e1 = g.add_node("make_line_redge", {"start": (0, 0, 0), "end": (1, 0, 0)})
    e2 = g.add_node("make_line_redge", {"start": (1, 0, 0), "end": (1, 1, 0)})
    wire = g.add_node("make_wire_from_edges_rwire", {"edge_count": 2}, inputs=[e1, e2])
    assert wire.node_id == g.leaf_nodes()[0].node_id

A *namespace* prefixes every id the graph allocates
(``<namespace>_node_00000001``). Graphs that share a ``graph_id`` but
allocate ids independently, such as the per-cell graphs of a notebook,
use distinct namespaces so their nodes can later meet in one graph
(:meth:`adopt`) without id clashes.
OperationNode:
A single node in the operation DAG.

Attributes:
    node_id:      Unique identifier within the graph.
    op:           Operation type (e.g. ``"make_line_redge"``, ``"make_cut_rsolid"``).
    params:       Serialisable parameters for re-creation.
    inputs:       Upstream nodes whose outputs feed into this node.
    context:      Work-plane / coordinate-system snapshot taken at creation time.
    output_count: Number of output shapes this node produces (usually 1).
    topo_delta:   Topological change set (may be ``None`` for simple primitives).
    tags:         Free-form labels for annotation.
    source:       Best-effort Python source provenance; ignored by replay.
    expressions:  The expressions ``param_exprs`` refers to.
    frame:        The coordinate frame current when the node was recorded.

``expressions`` and ``frame`` duplicate what the recording session keeps
in its expression and frame graphs. They travel with the node so a node
that outlives its session (a notebook cell's result, restored from the
cell cache) can still be registered in a new one. They are excluded from
equality and from :meth:`OperationGraph.to_dict`.

Return a semantic shape view with a canonical tag assignment.

second naming system.  Tags resolve through the recorded history, so a tagged face
keeps its name through later features (``ql.tag(...)`` and

assert_blend_volume_monotonic:
Mechanism E exit check: an all-convex blend may only remove material.

Observed kernel behavior (and the reason this check exists): filleting
every edge of a 10 mm cube with r=6 *succeeds* and returns a solid whose
volume (1036.35) exceeds the input (1000) — geometrically impossible
output that the kernel hands back without a word.  Fillet and chamfer
outputs on convex edges are subsets of the input solid, so a volume
increase beyond measurement noise means the kernel silently produced
garbage; we name it instead of returning it.

The increase check only fires for provably all-convex selections:
blending a *concave* edge legitimately adds material (the corner fill —
e.g. a bolt's underhead fillet gains exactly the quarter-circle deficit
times its circumference), and undeterminable edges mean the check
cannot prove impossibility.  A non-positive result volume is garbage
regardless of convexity and always fires.

The check runs on the success path, so it must stay cheap: two GProp
volume evaluations plus one side-probe per selected edge.  Raised as a
``BlendVolumeViolation`` so the caller's ``_wrap_blend_failure`` handler
promotes the measured facts and layers the standard blend diagnosis
(probes, evidence render) on top.

leg at ``distance * tan(angle)`` on the non-reference side;
``reference_direction`` picks, per edge, the adjacent face whose outward
normal best matches it as the reference face.

diagnose_blend_failure:
Classify a fillet/chamfer failure; never raises.

Probe order (cheapest explanation wins):

1. Tangent adjacency — the two faces meeting at a selected edge are
   already tangent (dihedral ~180°), so the blend surface degenerates to
   zero width regardless of size.
2. Room — blend size exceeds the distance from the edge to the opposite
   boundary of an adjacent face.
3. Interaction — per-edge diagnostic rerun (``retry_single``, capped at
   64 edges) isolates edges that fail alone; when every edge passes
   alone but the joint blend fails, opposite blends on a shared face
   meeting tangentially (2×size >= face room) is the explanation.
diagnose_boolean_failure:
Classify a boolean failure from its operands; never raises.

Model: operands within ``tol`` of each other form one connected cluster
(transitively). More than one cluster means the union is genuinely
separated — report the nearest inter-cluster pair. A single cluster that
still failed to fuse contains a touch-without-overlap pair — report it as
non-manifold contact. Returns None when no pair explains the failure.

draft_rsolid:
Draft planar, cylindrical or conical faces by a signed angle in degrees.

The neutral plane fixes the unchanged section: the selected faces lean
toward or away from it. Its origin and normal are in current
coordinate-system coordinates. Face selection is checked against the input
body and retained as graph inputs for strict replay. The input solid is
preserved, the output must be one valid solid, and a zero angle records an
unchanged result. Other surface families are explicitly rejected.

Extrude a planar face until a target surface, including curved surfaces.

The direction is interpreted in the current coordinate system and
normalized before construction. ``until`` selects the termination:
``NEXT`` (forward, nearest intersecting target surface), ``LAST`` (forward,
farthest), ``PREVIOUS`` (reverse, nearest) and ``FIRST`` (reverse,
farthest). The temporary prism is intersected with the target, the target's
boundary faces are taken from kernel history and sewn into surfaces, and
the prism is split on the selected one. Bounding boxes only size the
temporary prism; they do not define the termination surface, and side
walls parallel to the direction do not join separate near and far limits.

Targets must cover the profile at the requested contact: an uncovered,
open or disconnected output is rejected, as are a missing contact, an
invalid mode, a zero or nonfinite direction and an empty target sequence.
Inputs are preserved. The operation is recorded as
``make_extrude_until_rsolid``; its ordered inputs are the profile followed
by every target solid and its parameters keep ``direction``, ``until`` and
``target_count``, so a changed target is recomputed on replay (no final
BRep is embedded).

Args:
    profile: The planar face to extrude.
    target: A solid, or a sequence of solids, that bounds the extrusion.
    direction: Extrusion direction in current coordinate-system
        coordinates.
    until: ``"NEXT"``, ``"LAST"``, ``"PREVIOUS"`` or ``"FIRST"``.

Returns:
    One valid solid.

Raises:
    TypeError: ``profile`` is not a Face, or ``target`` is not a Solid or
        a sequence of Solid.
    ValueError: No target, no contact, insufficient coverage, a bad mode
        or direction, or an invalid kernel result.

    profile = scad.make_rectangle_rface(2, 2)
    ceiling = scad.make_box_rsolid(10, 10, 2, bottom_face_center=(0, 0, 5))
    near = scad.extrude_until_rsolid(profile, ceiling, until="NEXT")  # volume 20
    far = scad.extrude_until_rsolid(profile, ceiling, until="LAST")  # volume 28
    sphere = scad.make_sphere_rsolid(5, center=(0, 0, 10))
    curved = scad.extrude_until_rsolid(profile, sphere)

fit_cubic_bspline_control_points:
Fit a minimal cubic B-spline control polygon to sampled curve points.

Uses chord-length parameterization, cubic clamped B-spline least squares,
second-difference fairing regularization, and adaptive simple knot insertion
until the maximum sample error is within `tolerance`. Only simple interior
knots are inserted, so a cubic result remains C2-continuous at every interior
knot.

Args:
    sample_points: Ordered 2D or 3D points sampled along the intended curve.
        Consecutive duplicate points within `duplicate_tolerance` are ignored.
    tolerance: Maximum allowed Euclidean fitting error at the input samples.
    max_control_points: Upper bound for fitted control points. Defaults to the
        cleaned sample count, with a cubic minimum of four controls.
    fairing: Non-negative second-difference regularization weight. Larger
        values prefer smoother control polygons while still respecting the
        error tolerance when possible.
    duplicate_tolerance: Distance threshold for removing consecutive duplicate
        sample points before chord-length parameterization.
    knot_tolerance: Normalized parameter spacing threshold used to avoid
        duplicate or near-boundary interior knots.
    raise_on_failure: Raise `ValueError` when the tolerance cannot be reached
        within `max_control_points`. If false, return the best non-converged
        result instead.

Returns:
    `BSplineFitResult` containing cubic degree, control points, a full clamped
    knot vector, knot multiplicities, sample parameters, and fitting error.

Raises:
    ValueError: If inputs are invalid, or if the tolerance cannot be met and
        `raise_on_failure=True`.

Examples:
    ```python
    from simplecadapi.math import fit_cubic_bspline_control_points

    samples = [(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), (1.0, 0.4, 0.0), (2.0, 0.0, 0.0)]
    fit = fit_cubic_bspline_control_points(samples, tolerance=0.01)
    print(fit.control_points)
    print(fit.knots, fit.multiplicities)
    ```

Create a cycloidal reducer disc for a one-tooth-difference pin ring.

This is a single-disc geometric standard part. Real compact reducers often
stack two identical-lobe discs to balance output-pin side loads. In that
assembly-level pattern, separate two concepts that are easy to confuse:

- Place the two input eccentric cam centers 180 degrees apart, for example
  ``(+e, 0)`` and ``(-e, 0)``, so their orbit loads oppose each other.
- Tooth-index the second cycloidal profile by half a lobe, not by a full
  180 degree shape rotation. For a disc with ``n_lobes`` lobes, that
  geometric body phase is ``180 / n_lobes`` degrees. A 10-lobe disc rotated
  by 180 degrees is exactly five full lobe pitches and is visually and
  mechanically equivalent to no tooth-index phase change.

If output-pin clearance holes must stay aligned to one shared output pin
set, compensate the second disc's ``output_pin_phase`` by subtracting the
same body phase before rotating the finished disc body.

----------

    Number of cycloidal lobes. The matching fixed pin ring has
    ``n_lobes + 1`` pins and gives a single-stage ``n_lobes:1`` reduction.
ring_pin_pitch_radius : float
    Radius of the fixed ring pin centers in mm.
roller_radius : float
    Radius of the fixed ring pins or rollers used to offset the profile.
eccentricity : float
    Input crank eccentricity in mm.
gear_height : float, default 6.0
    Disc thickness / extrusion height along Z in mm.
bore_radius : float, default 0.0
    Optional central bore radius. Zero leaves the disc unbored.
output_pin_count : int, default 0
    Optional number of circular output-pin clearance holes.
output_pin_pitch_radius : float, default 0.0
    Radius of the output-pin clearance hole centers in mm.
output_pin_clearance_radius : float, default 0.0
    Radius of each output-pin clearance hole in mm.
output_pin_phase : float, default 0.0
    Angular phase of the first output-pin clearance hole in degrees, in the
    unrotated disc's local frame. When a finished disc is rotated to create
    a tooth-index phase in a twin-disc stack, subtract that same rotation
    from ``output_pin_phase`` if the clearance holes should remain aligned
    to the same global output pins.
sample_count_per_lobe : int, default 33
    Number of analytic samples fitted into each lobe B-spline segment.
spline_tolerance : float, default 0.005
    Cubic B-spline fit tolerance in mm.

    Maximum poles allowed for each fitted lobe segment.

the failure-marking channel used by the blend diagnostics.

trim_rsketch:
Remove the part of a line, circle, arc or B-spline that contains ``at``, between the nearest cuts.

A cut is a crossing with another non-construction line, circle, arc, ellipse or B-spline (``against`` limits
which ones) or an end of the entity; a tangent touch is one cut. ``at`` is a point (x, y) in sketch coordinates
or a point id. Lines, arcs and open B-splines keep the pieces on either side; a circle keeps the arc left over and
a closed B-spline (periodic, or starting and ending on one point) the piece left over (both need two cuts); an
entity nothing crosses is removed whole. A B-spline piece is a new B-spline (ids s1, s2, ...) of the same curve:
its first and last control points are its end points, its inner control points are sketch points (an original
control point the piece keeps unmoved keeps its id, the others are new points p1, p2, ...), and its knots are no
longer uniform. Cut points are tied to the cutter with point_on; line pieces inherit horizontal/vertical;
constraints on an end point stay with the piece that keeps that point, a tangent at a B-spline end (at_a/at_b)
moves to the piece that keeps that end, other constraints that name the removed entity are removed, and so are
the original control points no piece uses, with their constraints. Use diff_sketch_rsketchdiff(before, after) to
see what changed.
insert_spline_anchor_rsketch:
Insert an anchor into a B-spline in anchor form, at the curve point nearest ``at``, without changing the curve.

The anchor form is a pen tool's curve: anchors on the curve, each with an in-handle and an out-handle. It is a cubic
B-spline whose control points are ``[A0, out0, in1, A1, out1, in2, A2, ...]`` (every one a sketch point) and whose
inner knots have multiplicity 3, so every span is a cubic Bezier from one anchor to the next; the editor's spline tool
draws them, ``convert_spline_to_anchors_rsketch`` turns another B-spline into one. Moving an anchor or a handle is
moving its point (the solver moves every control point of such a spline).

The span under ``at`` is split at that place (de Casteljau), so the curve is the same: the span's two handles get
shorter (they keep their ids; a dimension or fix on them no longer holds and is dropped, see the notes) and the new
anchor and its two handles are new points ``p<n>`` (the lowest free numbers). The new knot is the curve parameter of
the place, with multiplicity 3. ``at`` is a point (x, y) in sketch coordinates or a point id. The sketch is solved
first. Refused for a B-spline that is not in anchor form and at an existing anchor. Metadata ``last_edit`` notes name
the new anchor and its handles; ``diff_sketch_rsketchdiff(before, after)`` lists them too.
remove_spline_anchor_rsketch:
Remove an inner anchor (and its two handles) from a B-spline in anchor form.

``anchor`` is the point id of an anchor that is not an end. The spans on either side become one span: its handles are
the outer handles of the two spans, which keep their ids and directions and get the lengths that fit the old curve best
(least squares, never reversed), so removing an anchor that ``insert_spline_anchor_rsketch`` made gives back the curve
it split. A handle that a constraint or another entity holds keeps its place. The removed points are deleted unless
another entity uses them, and the constraints on deleted points are dropped (the notes of metadata ``last_edit`` name
them). Refused for an end anchor, a handle, a point that is not on the spline, and a B-spline not in anchor form.
convert_spline_to_anchors_rsketch:
Write a B-spline in anchor form (Bezier spans: anchors on the curve, a handle on each side).

A non-rational B-spline of degree 3 or less keeps its exact shape (degree elevation and knot insertion); a rational one
or one of a higher degree is approximated within 1e-4 and the notes of metadata ``last_edit`` say how close. The end
points keep their ids; an inner control point that does not move keeps its id, the others are new points ``p<n>``, and
control points no entity uses any more are deleted with their constraints. A B-spline already in anchor form is left
as it is (a note says so). Refused for a periodic B-spline. See ``insert_spline_anchor_rsketch`` for the form.
trim_surface_face: Project 3D wires onto a carrier and return one trimmed face.
trim_surface_rface:
Trim a carrier Face to exactly one connected Face.

Existing carrier bounds and holes are preserved by intersecting them with
the requested closed, simple outer loop and optional closed, simple holes.
Empty or disconnected intersections are rejected. Every trim curve must
lie on the carrier within ``tolerance``. Periodic carriers do not support
holes; their outer loop must fit within one seam period without crossing
the seam.
twisted_sweep_rsolid:
Sweep a planar profile along a straight axis with linear rotation.

``twist_angle`` is the signed total rotation in degrees. The operation uses
a cylindrical auxiliary spine to define a continuous rotation law, yielding
one continuous side face per profile edge instead of a segmented ruled loft.
union_rsolid:
Compute the boolean union and return one manifold solid.

Face-area contact and positive-volume overlap can produce one solid without
artificial embedding. Edge-only, vertex-only, and point/curve tangencies
are non-manifold connections and cannot satisfy the one-Solid contract.

``glue`` is an OCC optimization for compatible touching or coincident
topology, not a geometry repair switch. If the optimized pass does not
return one solid, SimpleCAD automatically retries the normal fuse algorithm.

Args:
    solids: One or more Solid objects or sequences of Solid. Nested sequences are
        flattened before processing.
    clean: Unify same-domain faces and remove splitter edges when possible.
    glue: Try OCC glue optimization first, then fall back to normal fuse if
        necessary. Defaults to False.
    tol: Optional finite non-negative fuzzy-boolean tolerance used by OCC. It
        may intentionally bridge a small gap but cannot make a non-manifold
        point or edge contact into a valid solid.
    tracking_policy: FULL computes topology history and lineage. GRAPH keeps
        the replayable operation node without computing a TopoDelta.

Returns:
    Solid: The merged union result.

Usage:
    Accepts standalone `Solid` objects, lists of `Solid`, and nested sequences,
    but always returns exactly one `Solid`. If the kernel cannot produce
    exactly one solid result, the API raises a clear error instead of
    returning multiple pieces.

Examples:
    body = make_box_rsolid(10, 4, 4, bottom_face_center=(0, 0, 0))
    rib = make_box_rsolid(2, 4, 4, bottom_face_center=(4, 0, 0))
    merged = union_rsolid(body, rib)
    print(merged.get_volume())
unit_from_payload: Deserialize a registered unit symbol or a custom unit definition.
unit_to_payload: Serialize a unit compactly without losing custom unit definitions.
upstream_closure:
Return *roots* and every node upstream of them, inputs first.

The walk is an iterative depth-first post-order over ``inputs``, so
chains of any length are fine and the order is deterministic. Nodes are
identified by ``node_id``: a second object with an id already seen is
skipped when :func:`same_node_content` holds and raises
:class:`StaleLineageError` otherwise. Nodes for which *stop_at* returns
true are neither returned nor walked through.
user_tag_binding: Create a canonical user assertion with explicit frozen policies.
validate_placement_ticks: Validate a persisted tick frame with exact integer arithmetic.
value:
Build a value key extractor for ordering and projection in QL.

Args:
    path: Property or metadata path to resolve.
    default: Fallback value when the path is missing.

Returns:
    Serializable key function for `Query.order_by(...)`.
var:
Create a physical or legacy scalar variable.

``tolerance=0.1`` declares a symmetric ``+/-0.1`` tolerance. Use a
``(lower_deviation, upper_deviation)`` pair for an asymmetric tolerance.
``tolerance_unit`` defaults to ``unit`` when a nominal unit is declared.
Values are converted to canonical CAD units only when evaluated, so the
declaration and serialized expression node preserve the user's units.

Variables without ``unit`` retain legacy unitless behavior. A unit-aware
expression cannot mix declared-unit variables with legacy variables.
cut_rsolid_list:
Compute the boolean difference of solids and keep every piece.

A cut can split the body (a slot through a bar leaves two parts) or consume it
(a tool that encloses the whole body leaves nothing). ``cut_rsolid`` refuses
such a result because it returns exactly one ``Solid``; this operator returns
them all. A tool is cut from every piece it meets, so several tools may split
a body into several parts.

Args:
    solids: One or more Solid objects or sequences of Solid. Nested sequences are
        flattened before processing; the first solid is the base, the rest are
        subtracted in order.
    skip_non_intersecting: When True, a tool that meets none of the current
        pieces is ignored; when False it raises.
    tracking_policy: FULL computes topology history and lineage. GRAPH keeps
        the replayable operation node without computing a TopoDelta.

Returns:
    list[Solid]: Every piece of the cut, in kernel order; empty when the tools
    consume the base.

Raises:
    SimpleCADError: An input is not a valid Solid, or the kernel could not
        compute the cut.

Usage:
    ``pieces = cut_rsolid_list(bar, slot)`` returns both halves of a bar cut by
    a through slot. Use ``cut_rsolid`` when the result must be one solid.
Body:
One named solid of a Part.

``Body(body_id, solid, name=None, color=None, opacity=None)``: ``body_id`` is an
identifier unique within the part, ``solid`` the body's Solid, ``name`` an optional
display name, ``color`` an optional display colour (RGB floats in [0, 1]) and
``opacity`` an optional display opacity in [0, 1]. A one-body Part has one Body with
the id ``"body"``. The colour overrides the Part's material colour for display only;
set it on an existing Part with ``set_body_appearance_rpart``.
measure_part_mass_rmassreport:
Measure the volume, mass and centre of mass of a Part.

Args:
    part: The Part to measure.
    density: Density to use instead of the material's; ``None`` uses the
        Part's material, and without a material density every mass is ``None``.
    density_unit: Unit of ``density``: ``kg/m^3`` (default), ``g/cm^3``,
        ``kg/mm^3`` or ``g/mm^3``.

Returns:
    MassReport: ``bodies`` (the Part's one ``BodyMass``: ``body_id``, ``volume_mm3``,
    ``mass_kg``, ``centroid_mm``) and the totals of the part (``volume_mm3``,
    ``mass_kg``, ``centroid_mm``).

Raises:

    ``scad.measure_part_mass_rmassreport(bracket).mass_kg`` is the mass of the part.
    The part's material gives the density unless ``density`` is passed.
inspect_curve_rcurvedata:
Read the NURBS data of an edge's curve: what the curve edits work on.

Returns ``{type, analytic, editable, conversion, degree, poles, weights, knots, multiplicities, periodic, rational, closed, domain, reversed, parameter_range}``. ``poles`` are points in the current coordinate system, indices are 0-based (the ``moves`` of ``move_curve_poles_redge``); ``parameter_range`` is the edge's own range (where ``insert_curve_knot_redge`` may insert). For a line, circle or other analytic curve ``editable`` is false, ``conversion`` is ``"convert_to_bspline_redge"`` and the data is what that conversion would produce. Not recorded in the graph.
inspect_surface_rsurfacedata:
Read the NURBS data of a face's surface: what the surface edits work on.

Returns ``{type, analytic, editable, conversion, u_degree, v_degree, poles, weights, u_knots, v_knots, u_multiplicities, v_multiplicities, u_periodic, v_periodic, rational, domain, reversed, trimmed, uv_bounds}``. ``poles`` is a grid of rows along U, each row running along V (as ``make_bezier_surface_rface`` takes it), in the current coordinate system; indices are 0-based ``(row, column)``. ``domain`` is the surface's ``[u1, u2, v1, v2]``, ``uv_bounds`` the face's; ``trimmed`` says whether the face is bounded by anything but the surface's own domain. For a plane, cylinder or other analytic surface ``editable`` is false, ``conversion`` is ``"convert_to_bspline_rface"`` and the data is what that conversion would produce. Not recorded in the graph.
convert_to_bspline_redge:
Convert an edge's curve to a B-spline, so the curve edits can work on it.

The explicit, recorded step for analytic edges (a line becomes a degree-1 B-spline, a circle or arc a rational quadratic); the shape does not change, its parameter range may. Returns a new Edge; the input is not changed. Recorded: the Edge continues in the node's history, so tags and references follow.
convert_to_bspline_rface:
Convert a face's surface (and its boundary curves) to B-splines, so the surface edits can work on it.

The explicit, recorded step for analytic faces (planes, cylinders, cones, spheres, ...); the shape and the trimming do not change, the (u, v) parametrisation may. Returns a new Face; the input is not changed. Recorded: the Face and its boundary edges continue in the node's history, so tags and references follow.
set_curve_poles_redge:
Set every pole of an edge's B-spline curve.

``poles`` lists exactly as many points as the curve has poles (``inspect_curve_rcurvedata``), in order, in the current coordinate system. Degree, knots and weights stay. Only B-spline and Bezier curves are edited; a line, circle or other analytic edge is refused with a message naming ``convert_to_bspline_redge``, the explicit conversion step. Returns a new Edge; the input is not changed. Recorded: the Edge continues in the node's history, so tags and references follow.
move_curve_poles_redge:
Move some poles of an edge's B-spline curve: ``moves`` maps a 0-based pole index to its new position.

The sparse form of ``set_curve_poles_redge`` (what a control-point drag records). Only B-spline and Bezier curves are edited; a line, circle or other analytic edge is refused with a message naming ``convert_to_bspline_redge``, the explicit conversion step. Returns a new Edge; the input is not changed. Recorded: the Edge continues in the node's history, so tags and references follow.
set_curve_weights_redge:
Set the weights of an edge's B-spline curve: one positive value per pole.

A weight above 1 pulls the curve toward its pole; any weight other than 1 makes the curve rational. Only B-spline and Bezier curves are edited; a line, circle or other analytic edge is refused with a message naming ``convert_to_bspline_redge``, the explicit conversion step. Returns a new Edge; the input is not changed. Recorded: the Edge continues in the node's history, so tags and references follow.
insert_curve_knot_redge:
Insert a knot into an edge's B-spline curve at ``parameter`` (strictly inside the edge's parameter range).

The shape does not change; the curve gains ``multiplicity`` poles near that parameter, for finer local editing. The knot's total multiplicity may not exceed the degree. Only B-spline and Bezier curves are edited; a line, circle or other analytic edge is refused with a message naming ``convert_to_bspline_redge``, the explicit conversion step. Returns a new Edge; the input is not changed. Recorded: the Edge continues in the node's history, so tags and references follow.
elevate_curve_degree_redge:
Raise the degree of an edge's B-spline curve to ``degree``.

The shape does not change; poles are added. Only B-spline and Bezier curves are edited; a line, circle or other analytic edge is refused with a message naming ``convert_to_bspline_redge``, the explicit conversion step. Returns a new Edge; the input is not changed. Recorded: the Edge continues in the node's history, so tags and references follow.
set_surface_poles_rface:
Set every pole of a face's B-spline surface.

``poles`` is the full grid (rows along U, each row along V), the same size as ``inspect_surface_rsurfacedata`` reports, in the current coordinate system. The face keeps its trimming exactly: its boundary loops stay where they are in the surface's (u, v) space and the 3D boundary edges are recomputed on the edited surface. Only B-spline and Bezier surfaces are edited; a plane, cylinder or other analytic face is refused with a message naming ``convert_to_bspline_rface``, the explicit conversion step. Returns a new Face; the input is not changed. Recorded: the Face and its boundary edges continue in the node's history, so tags and references follow.
move_surface_poles_rface:
Move some poles of a face's B-spline surface: ``moves`` maps a 0-based ``(row, column)`` to the pole's new position.

The sparse form of ``set_surface_poles_rface`` (what a control-point drag records). The face keeps its trimming exactly: its boundary loops stay where they are in the surface's (u, v) space and the 3D boundary edges are recomputed on the edited surface. Only B-spline and Bezier surfaces are edited; a plane, cylinder or other analytic face is refused with a message naming ``convert_to_bspline_rface``, the explicit conversion step. Returns a new Face; the input is not changed. Recorded: the Face and its boundary edges continue in the node's history, so tags and references follow.
set_surface_weights_rface:
Set the weights of a face's B-spline surface: a grid of positive values, one per pole.

The face keeps its trimming exactly: its boundary loops stay where they are in the surface's (u, v) space and the 3D boundary edges are recomputed on the edited surface. Only B-spline and Bezier surfaces are edited; a plane, cylinder or other analytic face is refused with a message naming ``convert_to_bspline_rface``, the explicit conversion step. Returns a new Face; the input is not changed. Recorded: the Face and its boundary edges continue in the node's history, so tags and references follow.
insert_surface_knot_rface:
Insert a U or V knot into a face's B-spline surface at ``parameter`` (strictly inside the surface's domain in that direction).

The shape does not change; the pole grid gains ``multiplicity`` rows (``"U"``) or columns (``"V"``). The face keeps its trimming exactly: its boundary loops stay where they are in the surface's (u, v) space and the 3D boundary edges are recomputed on the edited surface. Only B-spline and Bezier surfaces are edited; a plane, cylinder or other analytic face is refused with a message naming ``convert_to_bspline_rface``, the explicit conversion step. Returns a new Face; the input is not changed. Recorded: the Face and its boundary edges continue in the node's history, so tags and references follow.
elevate_surface_degree_rface:
Raise the U and/or V degree of a face's B-spline surface.

Give ``u_degree``, ``v_degree`` or both; a degree that is given is at least the current one and one of them is higher. The shape does not change; poles are added. The face keeps its trimming exactly: its boundary loops stay where they are in the surface's (u, v) space and the 3D boundary edges are recomputed on the edited surface. Only B-spline and Bezier surfaces are edited; a plane, cylinder or other analytic face is refused with a message naming ``convert_to_bspline_rface``, the explicit conversion step. Returns a new Face; the input is not changed. Recorded: the Face and its boundary edges continue in the node's history, so tags and references follow.
rebuild_curve_redge:
Refit an edge's curve as a B-spline of ``degree`` with ``pole_count`` poles, or with the fewest poles that keep within ``tolerance``.

A least-squares fit with uniform clamped knots in the edge's own parameter range; the end points are kept. Works on any edge, analytic ones too (the result is a B-spline). Returns a new Edge; the input is not changed. Recorded: the Edge continues in the node's history, so tags and references follow.
rebuild_surface_rface:
Refit a face's surface as a B-spline of the given degrees and pole counts, or with the fewest poles that keep within ``tolerance``.

Give both pole counts or neither. A least-squares fit in the face's own (u, v) parametrisation (over the surface's domain for a B-spline, over the face's bounds otherwise), so the face keeps its trimming. Works on any face. Returns a new Face; the input is not changed. Recorded: the Face and its boundary edges continue in the node's history, so tags and references follow.
sample_curve_rcurvature:
Sample an edge for a curvature comb: ``count`` points evenly in its parameter range.

Returns ``{parameters, points, tangents, normals, curvatures, max_curvature}`` in the current coordinate system; a normal points to the centre of curvature and is zero where the curve is straight. Not recorded in the graph.
sample_surface_risocurves:
Sample isocurves of a face, clipped to its trimming.

``u_count`` lines of constant u and ``v_count`` of constant v, evenly inside the face's (u, v) bounds, each sampled at ``samples`` points. Returns ``{u: [{parameter, segments}], v: [...], uv_bounds}``; ``segments`` are the runs of points that lie on the face. Not recorded in the graph.
set_body_appearance_rpart:
Set the display colour, opacity and display name of one body of a Part.

A Part is a value: the result is a new Part, the input is unchanged.  The colour is an
appearance only.  A body without a colour shows its Part's material colour
(``Material.color``), and without either it shows the default grey: the body colour
overrides the material colour for display (the live preview, the package scene, the STEP
surface colour of that solid).  Mass, density and geometry never read it.

Args:
    part: The Part (one body or several).
    body_id: The body to change: an id from ``part.body_ids()``. A one-body Part has
        the one body ``"body"`` (the default).
    color: Display colour as RGB floats in [0.0, 1.0], e.g. ``(0.8, 0.2, 0.2)``;
        linear RGB, as ``Material.color``, OpenCASCADE (so STEP) and three.js read
        it (the editor's colour picker converts its sRGB ``#rrggbb``). ``None``
        keeps the body's colour.
    opacity: Display opacity in [0.0, 1.0] (1 is opaque). ``None`` keeps it. STEP
        export writes the colour, not the opacity.
    name: Display name of the body (the editor's bodies list, the scene node,
        the STEP solid). ``None`` keeps it. The ``body_id`` never changes.
    reset: Clear the colour, opacity and name first, so the body shows the material
        colour, opaque, under its id; then apply what is given.

Returns:
    Part: The Part with that body's appearance changed; ``part.get_body(body_id).color``,
    ``.opacity`` and ``.name`` read it back.

Raises:
    SimpleCADError: The value is not a Part, the part has no such body, the colour is
        not three numbers in [0, 1], the opacity is outside [0, 1], or the name is empty.

Usage:
    ``case = scad.set_body_appearance_rpart(case, "lid", color=(0.9, 0.3, 0.2), name="Lid")``
    paints the lid body of a multi-body part; ``scad.set_body_appearance_rpart(part,
    color=(0.2, 0.4, 0.8))`` paints a one-body part. Recorded and replayed like
    ``assign_material_rpart``. To name a face or an edge for people, tag it
    (``scad.apply_tag_rselection`` / ``ql.tag``): a tag is the name.
make_workplane_rworkplane:

make_workplane_normal_to_curve_rworkplan:

    curve: An Edge or a Wire (the sweep path).
    at: The fraction of the length, in [0, 1].
    x_dir: The direction of x, projected onto the plane.

Returns:
    SimpleWorkplane: a frame in world coordinates (``origin``, ``normal``, ``x_dir``, ``y_dir``, ``plane``) that is
    also a context manager: ``with wp:`` makes it the current coordinate system, ``make_sketch_rsketch(plane=wp)``
    draws on it. It is a value: enter it again in later code, pickle it (the notebook cell cache does).

Raises:
    SimpleCADError: ``at`` is outside [0, 1], the curve has no length, or ``x_dir`` is along the tangent.

Usage:
    ``start = scad.make_workplane_normal_to_curve_rworkplane(path, 0)``;
    ``profile = ... make_sketch_rsketch("profile", plane=start) ...``; ``sweep_rsolid(profile, path)``.
list_tag_splits:
The tagged entities that the operations behind a shape split into pieces.

A tag follows its entity the way a reference does: while the entity stays one entity it keeps the tag; when an
operation splits it (a slot cut across a tagged face, a cut through a tagged body), the tag does not go to every
piece. Each piece carries ``<tag>.split1`` .. ``<tag>.split<n>`` instead, numbered as the operation recorded them (by
centre, then size), and ``ql.tag("<tag>")`` finds none of them. Name the pieces you mean with tags of your own after the
split, or select them with ``ql.tag("<tag>.split1")`` / ``ql.tag("<tag>.*")``.

Args:
    shape: A shape made in a recording session (its history is read).

Returns:
    list[dict]: One row per split, upstream first: ``tag`` (the tag the entity had), ``into`` (the tags of the pieces,
    in piece order), ``node_id`` and ``op`` (the operation that split it), ``source_topo_id`` and ``pieces``
    (``output_slot``, ``kind``, ``topo_id`` of each piece in that operation's output). Empty for a shape without
    recorded history.

Examples:
    >>> top = scad.apply_tag_rselection(box, scad.ql.faces().where(scad.ql.prop("geom.center.z", ">=", 9.9)), "mount.top")
    >>> halves = scad.cut_rsolid(top, slot)              # the slot splits the top face (and the body)
    >>> [row["into"] for row in scad.list_tag_splits(halves[0])]
    [['mount.top.split1', 'mount.top.split2']]
make_workplane_offset_rworkplane:
Create a workplane moved and turned relative to a workplane or a named plane.

The editor's move and turn handles write this operation: a plane placed by hand on a base, without any model geometry.

Args:
    base: The plane it is placed on: a workplane value (made by a ``make_workplane_*_rworkplane`` operation, recorded
        as this node's input so the new plane follows it when it moves) or a named plane ``"XY"`` / ``"XZ"`` / ``"YZ"``
        (axes as sketches read them).
    offset: How far the origin moves, ``(dx, dy, dz)`` along the base's own x, y and normal.
    rx, ry, rz: Turns in degrees about the base's own axes, applied in that order, each about the axis as the previous
        turn left it (R = Rx(rx) Ry(ry) Rz(rz) in the base's frame).

Returns:
    SimpleWorkplane: The new frame. Use it as a sketch plane (``plane=wp``) or as a context (``with wp:``).

Examples:
    >>> wp = scad.make_workplane_offset_rworkplane("XY", offset=(0, 0, 20), rx=30)
    >>> lid = scad.make_workplane_offset_rworkplane(wp, offset=(0, 0, 5))   # follows wp
inset_face_rsolid:
Imprint the loops of one planar face moved a distance inside it.

The outline of the face (and the outline of each of its holes) is offset in
the face's plane by ``distance`` towards the inside, and the offset loops are
imprinted on the solid: the face becomes an inner face and the ring around it
(a ring around each hole too).  The solid keeps its shape and volume; it only
has one face more, which the next operation can pull out, push in or open, so
steps, bosses and walls are built by insetting and pulling again.

The operation is recorded as ``make_inset_face_rsolid``; the body and the face
are ordered inputs and the distance is a parameter, so model JSON replay is
strict.  The split pieces are fragments of the face (element references and
tags follow them as a split) and carry the kernel roles ``inset.inner`` and
``inset.ring``, so ``scad.ref.face(..., role="inset.inner")`` names the inner
face whatever the face was.

Args:
    solid: The body whose face is inset.
    face: One planar face of ``solid``, or a QL selector that picks exactly one.
    distance: How far inside the face the loops run, in mm; positive.

Returns:
    The same solid with the face split in its inner face and ring.

Raises:
    TypeError: ``solid`` is not a Solid.
    ValueError: Not exactly one face, a face of another solid, a curved
        face, a non-positive distance, or a distance at which nothing of the
        face is left inside the loops.

Examples:
    import simplecadapi as scad
    ql = scad.ql
    box = scad.make_box_rsolid(40, 30, 20)
    top = ql.faces().where(ql.prop("geom.center.z", ">=", 19.9)).exactly(1)
    inset = scad.inset_face_rsolid(box, top, 3)
    inner = scad.ref.face("", "make_inset_face_rsolid", role="inset.inner").one(inset)
press_pull_rsolid:
Pull one planar face out along its normal, or press it in.

A positive ``distance`` pulls the face out: the prism of the face along its
outward normal is joined to the solid (a boss, a step).  A negative one presses
it in: the prism into the solid is cut (a pocket, a recess; through the solid it
cuts a hole).  Zero leaves the solid as it is.  One signed number covers both, so
a parameter can be tuned across zero without changing the code.

Pair it with ``inset_face_rsolid``: inset a face, then press or pull its inner
face, to build steps, bosses and walls without a sketch.

The operation is recorded as its steps: ``make_extrude_rsolid`` of the face,
then ``make_union_rsolid`` (pull) or ``make_cut_rsolid`` (press), so the new
faces carry the extrusion's roles (``extrusion.end`` is the moved face,
``extrusion.side`` its walls) and element references follow them.

Args:
    solid: The body whose face is pressed or pulled.
    face: One planar face of ``solid``, or a QL selector that picks exactly one.
    distance: How far, in mm, along the face's outward normal: positive pulls,
        negative presses.

Returns:
    The solid with the face pulled out or pressed in.

Raises:
    TypeError: ``solid`` is not a Solid.
    ValueError: Not exactly one face, a face of another solid, a curved face,
        a non-finite distance, or a press that removes the whole solid.

Examples:
    import simplecadapi as scad
    ql = scad.ql
    box = scad.make_box_rsolid(40, 30, 20)
    top = ql.faces().where(ql.prop("geom.center.z", ">=", 19.9)).exactly(1)
    stepped = scad.inset_face_rsolid(box, top, 3)
    inner = scad.ref.faces(scad.ref.face("", "make_inset_face_rsolid", role="inset.inner"))
    boss = scad.press_pull_rsolid(stepped, inner, 10)
    pocket = scad.press_pull_rsolid(stepped, inner, -4)
